corpus_definition: Feeling a strong need for help because of a very bad situation.

forms.definition: the feeling of being ready to do anything because things are very bad
forms.example: In desperation, he called his old friend and asked for money.

syn.note: Related: the feeling that nothing will get better; desperation often makes you act fast.
Related: sudden strong fear that stops you thinking clearly.

ant.note: Hope is the feeling that things will get better.

forms.note: No verb is made from desperate. The verb despair shares the same old Latin root but is a separate word.

forms.definition: needing help very much because a situation is very bad
forms.example: The family was desperate for clean water after the flood.

syn.note: Related: hopeless means you think nothing can help; desperate people still try hard.
Related: very worried and acting quickly without order.
Related: urgent describes a need that must be met now, not a person's feeling.

ant.note: Calm people are relaxed and not worried.

forms.definition: in a way that shows great need or worry
forms.example: She desperately wanted to find her lost cat.

syn.note: Related: 'I badly need help' is close to 'I desperately need help'.
Related: very quickly because something is needed now.

ant.note: In a relaxed way, without worry.

context.text: After losing his job, Akmal was desperate for work. He desperately called every company in Tashkent, and in desperation he even asked his old teacher for help.

reviewer_note: Root trap: despair (verb/noun) shares the Latin root but is not made from desperate, so it is in not_family, not a form or synonym.

corpus_definition: a form of a language spoken in one region or by one group

forms.definition: a form of a language that people speak in one area or group
forms.example: People in that village speak an old local dialect.

syn.note: Related: an accent is only about how words sound; a dialect also has its own words and grammar.
Related: language experts use 'variety' for any form of a language.
Related: a language is the whole system; a dialect is one form of it.

forms.note: No verb exists in this family.

forms.definition: connected with the way people speak in one area or group
forms.example: The old songs are full of dialectal words from the region.
forms.note: Mostly used by language experts and teachers.

syn.note: Related: from or about one part of a country.
Related: from the area where you are; easier, everyday word.

ant.note: The standard form of a language is the one taught in schools and used on the news.

forms.note: The adverb dialectally is very rare and not in learner dictionaries.

context.text: My grandmother speaks a dialect from Khorezm. Some dialectal words she uses are hard for people in Tashkent to understand.

reviewer_note: dialectic/dialectical (logic, argument) look similar but are not made from dialect; left out.

corpus_definition: working very hard and carefully over a long time

forms.definition: careful and steady effort in your work or studies
forms.example: Her diligence helped her pass every exam with high marks.

syn.note: Everyday phrase with almost the same meaning.
Related: effort is the energy you use; diligence means effort over a long time.
Related: paying attention so you don't make mistakes.

ant.note: Laziness is not wanting to work.

forms.note: No verb exists in this family.

forms.definition: working hard and carefully for a long time
forms.example: The diligent student reviewed her notes every evening.

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning. Also spelled hard-working.
Formal: careful to do your work well and correctly.
Formal and a little old-fashioned: always busy working.
Related: careful is about avoiding mistakes, not about working long hours.
Related: doing every part of a job completely.

ant.note: A lazy person doesn't want to work.
A careless person doesn't pay attention and makes mistakes.

forms.definition: in a hard-working and careful way
forms.example: He diligently checked every page of the report.

syn.note: Related: carefully is about attention; diligently also means working hard for a long time.
Related: 'work hard' is the everyday way to say it.

ant.note: In a way that shows you don't want to work.
Without paying attention.

context.text: Malika is a diligent student. She studies diligently every evening, and her diligence helped her win a place at university in Samarkand.

reviewer_note: No affix claimed for diligence (-ent/-ence swap, no free stem).

corpus_definition: To think that something or someone is wrong or bad.

forms.definition: the feeling that something or someone is wrong or bad
forms.example: She shook her head in disapproval when she saw the mess.

syn.note: Related: criticism is saying what is wrong; disapproval can be only a feeling or a look.
Related: a reason you give for not agreeing with something.
Related: not liking something, but not always thinking it is wrong.

ant.note: Approval is the feeling that something is good or right.

forms.definition: to think that something or someone is bad or wrong
forms.example: My parents strongly disapprove of my new hobby.
forms.note: Usually followed by 'of': disapprove of something.

syn.note: Related: you say you don't agree; often 'object to something'.
Related: you say what is wrong. British spelling: criticise.
Related: you don't like it, but you may not think it is wrong.
Phrasal verb with almost the same meaning: 'My school frowns on mobile phones.'

ant.note: To think that something is good or right: 'My parents approve of my friends.'

forms.definition: showing that you think someone has done something bad
forms.example: My aunt gave me a disapproving look when I arrived late.

syn.note: Very close: saying or showing that something is wrong.

ant.note: Showing that you think something is good.

forms.definition: in a way that shows you think something is wrong
forms.example: The teacher looked disapprovingly at my phone.

syn.note: Related: in a way that shows what is wrong.

ant.note: In a way that shows you think something is good.

context.text: My father disapproves of long hair on boys. When my brother came home with long hair, Dad gave him a disapproving look, but he kept his disapproval to himself.

reviewer_note: Headword already has the negative prefix; approve/approval/approving are given as antonyms, not forms.

corpus_definition: The ability to control your behavior to achieve something.

forms.definition: the ability to control yourself and keep working towards a goal
forms.example: He has the discipline to practice daily.
forms.note: Discipline also means punishment and rules (school discipline) and a subject of study; those are other meanings.

syn.note: Almost the same: controlling what you do and feel.
Very close: the strength to make yourself do difficult things.
Related: not giving up; discipline is more about daily habits.

ant.note: A lack of control over how people behave.

forms.definition: to train yourself to control what you do
forms.example: I discipline myself to study for an hour every morning.
forms.note: Often 'discipline yourself to do something'. It can also mean to punish someone, which is another meaning.

syn.note: Related: to teach yourself or others a skill or habit.
Related: to make something do what you want.

forms.definition: able to control your behaviour and work in a planned way
forms.example: She is a very disciplined runner who trains every day.

syn.note: Related: giving all your attention to one goal.
Related: planning your work well. British spelling: organised.

ant.note: Not able to control your behaviour or keep good habits.

forms.definition: connected with punishing people who break rules
forms.example: The company took disciplinary action against the driver.
forms.note: Belongs to discipline = punishment and rules, not self-control.
No adverb exists in this family.

people.definition: a person who believes in strict rules and punishment
people.example: Our old head teacher was a strict disciplinarian.
people.note: Belongs to discipline = rules and punishment, not self-control.

context.text: Learning the dutar takes discipline. My brother is very disciplined: he disciplines himself to practise every evening after dinner.

reviewer_note: Three meanings (self-control / punishment / subject of study); map keeps self-control, disciplinary and disciplinarian marked other_meaning.

corpus_definition: to make someone feel less confident or less willing to do something

forms.definition: a feeling that you have less hope or confidence
forms.example: Despite the discouragement of failing twice, she kept training.

syn.note: Related: the sad feeling when something is not as good as you hoped.
Related but much stronger: losing all hope.

ant.note: Words or actions that give someone confidence and hope.

forms.definition: to make someone less confident or less willing to do something
forms.example: Constant criticism can discourage even the best students.
forms.note: It can also mean to try to stop something happening: 'discourage smoking'.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal.
Everyday British phrasal verb: 'The rain put us off going out.'
Related: to make someone feel sad.

ant.note: To give someone confidence or hope to do something.
To make someone want to do something.

forms.definition: feeling that you have lost confidence or hope
forms.example: He felt discouraged after failing the driving test.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal.
Related: sad because something was not as good as you hoped.

ant.note: Feeling more confident and hopeful.

forms.definition: making you feel less confident or hopeful
forms.example: The first results of the experiment were discouraging.

syn.note: Related: not as good as you hoped.
Related: making you feel sad.

ant.note: Making you feel more confident and hopeful.

forms.definition: in a way that makes you feel less hopeful
forms.example: The exam was discouragingly difficult for most of the class.

syn.note: Related: in a way that is not as good as you hoped.

ant.note: In a way that gives you hope or confidence.

context.text: Bad marks can discourage young learners. Our teacher knows this, so when a test result is discouraging, she talks to every student who feels discouraged.

reviewer_note: Opposite family (encourage, encouragement, encouraging) given as antonyms; no dis- affix claimed because courage is not a verb.

corpus_definition: To treat some people worse than others because of who they are.

forms.definition: unfair treatment of some people because of their race, sex, age or religion
forms.example: Discrimination against women at work is against the law.

syn.note: Related: an unfair opinion about a group; discrimination is the unfair action.
Related: unfairly preferring one person or group.
Related: easy general word for treatment that is not fair.
Related: discrimination because of race only.

ant.note: When all people are treated in the same fair way.

forms.definition: to treat some people worse than others because of who they are
forms.example: It is illegal to discriminate against people because of their age.
forms.note: Usually 'discriminate against someone'. 'Discriminate between' means to see the difference, which is another meaning.

syn.note: Related: to choose one person from a group, often to treat them badly.
Related: to keep someone out of a group or place.

forms.definition: treating some groups of people unfairly
forms.example: The new rule was discriminatory against older workers.

syn.note: Easy everyday word; discriminatory is more formal and about groups of people.
Very close: unfairly preferring one group.
Related: having unfair opinions about a group.

ant.note: Treating everyone in the same right way.

forms.definition: able to judge what is good quality
forms.example: She is a discriminating reader who only buys the best books.
forms.note: Belongs to discriminate = see the difference between things, not treating people unfairly.

forms.definition: without thinking carefully or choosing
forms.example: The soldiers fired indiscriminately into the crowd.
forms.note: Belongs to discriminate = see differences and choose carefully; it does not mean 'without unfair treatment'.

context.text: In some countries, companies discriminate against older workers. This kind of discrimination is illegal in many places, and discriminatory job adverts must be removed.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: the row's example sentence does not use 'discriminate'. Trap: discriminating / indiscriminately belong to the 'tell the difference' meaning.

corpus_definition: the loss of respect and honor due to shameful behaviour

forms.definition: the loss of other people's respect because of something bad you did
forms.example: His dishonesty brought disgrace upon his entire family.
forms.note: Also used for something very bad: 'This dirty street is a disgrace!'

syn.note: Very close and easier.
Formal. British spelling: dishonour.
Related: a feeling of being made to look stupid or weak.
Related: a public story about something very wrong.

ant.note: Great respect that people have for you. British spelling: honour.
The good opinion people have of you.

forms.definition: to make people lose respect for you or your family
forms.example: He disgraced his family by stealing money from his boss.

syn.note: Very close: 'He shamed his family.'
Related: to make someone feel silly or uncomfortable; much weaker.
Related: to make someone feel stupid or weak in front of others.

forms.definition: so bad that people should feel ashamed
forms.example: The way they treated the old man was disgraceful.

syn.note: Same meaning.
Very close, often about public behaviour.
Related: easy general word for very bad.
Related: so bad that it makes people angry.

ant.note: So good that people respect it.

forms.definition: having lost other people's respect because of something bad
forms.example: The disgraced minister left the country.

syn.note: Very close, but less common.

forms.definition: in a very bad way that should make you ashamed
forms.example: The fans behaved disgracefully after the match.

syn.note: Same meaning.
Related: easy general word.

ant.note: In a very good way that people respect.

context.text: The footballer was sent home in disgrace after the fight. Fans called his behaviour disgraceful and said he had disgraced the national team.

reviewer_note: No dis- affix claimed: disgrace is not simply the opposite of grace. Corpus mixes US honor with UK behaviour; both spellings noted.

corpus_definition: Changing your look so that people do not recognize you.

forms.definition: clothes or other things you wear so people do not know who you are
forms.example: He wore a disguise to hide his face.
forms.note: Common phrase: 'in disguise' = wearing a disguise.

syn.note: Related: clothes you wear to look like someone else, often for a party or play.
Related: colours or covers that help something hide, used by soldiers and animals.
Related: covers only your face.

forms.definition: to change how someone or something looks so others cannot know them
forms.example: She disguised herself as an old woman to get past the guards.

syn.note: Related: to put something where people cannot see it.
Related: to cover or hide something, often a feeling or smell.
Related: to make something hard to see against its background.

ant.note: To show something that was hidden.

forms.definition: changed in the way it looks or sounds so people will not know it
forms.example: He phoned the police in a disguised voice.

syn.note: Close: wearing a mask or hidden.
Related: easy word for something you cannot see.

ant.note: Shown openly, not hidden: 'undisguised anger'.

forms.note: No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: For the school play, Bekzod wore a disguise: a big hat and a false beard. He was so well disguised that his own mother didn't know him, and he even disguised his voice.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: the definition reads like an action ('Changing your look') but the example uses the noun; map follows the noun with the verb as a conversion.

corpus_definition: To tell someone they are no longer needed at work.

forms.definition: the act of making someone leave their job
forms.example: His dismissal came as a shock to everyone in the office.

syn.note: Same meaning, informal British English.
Very close, everyday American English.
Related: losing your job because the job itself is no longer needed.

ant.note: Choosing someone for a job.

forms.definition: to make someone leave their job
forms.example: The company had to dismiss several workers.
forms.note: Dismiss also means to send people away (class dismissed) or to refuse to think about an idea.

syn.note: Same meaning, everyday and a little informal.
Same meaning, informal British English.
Polite way to say it: 'They let ten workers go.'
Related: workers lose their jobs because there is not enough work, not because of something they did.

ant.note: To give someone a job.
To pay someone to work for you.
To choose someone for an important job.

forms.definition: showing that you think something is not important
forms.example: He was very dismissive of my idea and didn't even listen.
forms.note: Belongs to dismiss = refuse to think about an idea, not making someone leave a job.

forms.definition: in a way that shows you think something is not important
forms.example: She waved her hand dismissively and walked away.
forms.note: Belongs to dismiss = refuse to think about an idea, not making someone leave a job.

context.text: The factory in Navoi dismissed ten workers last month. Their dismissal made the local news, and many people were angry.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: dismissive/dismissively belong to the 'refuse to consider' meaning, kept as other_meaning.

gate_overrides.msg_contains: 'dismissively' (other meaning): not in the dictionary as a adverb
gate_overrides.reason: dismissively is a headword adverb in the Oxford Advanced Learner's and Cambridge dictionaries (under dismissive); WordNet 3.1 lacks it.
